en: Vibhaṅga:
Analysis of the Immeasurables (Appamaññāvibhaṅga) 1.
The Exposition According to the Discourses (Suttantabhājanīya)
The four immeasurables:
here a bhikkhu dwells, having pervaded one quarter with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth.

Thus above, below, across, everywhere, and to all as to himself, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness—vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will.
He dwells pervading one quarter with a mind imbued with compassion, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth.

Thus, above, below, across, everywhere, and to all as to himself, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with compassion—vast, exalted, measureless, free from enmity, and free from ill will.
He dwells pervading one quarter with a mind imbued with sympathetic joy, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth.

Thus, above, below, across, and everywhere, to all as to himself, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with sympathetic joy—vast, exalted, measureless, free from enmity, and free from ill will.
With a mind imbued with equanimity, he dwells pervading one quarter; likewise the second, likewise the third, and likewise the fourth.

Thus, above, below, across, and everywhere, to all as to himself, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with equanimity— vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will.
And how does a bhikkhu dwell pervading one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness?
Just as one might feel loving-kindness upon seeing a person who is dear and pleasing,
even so does he pervade all beings with loving-kindness.
In this context, what is loving-kindness?
That which is loving-kindness toward beings, the state of being loving-kind, the state of having been loving-kind, and liberation of mind through loving-kindness—
this is called "loving-kindness.
In this context, what is the mind?
That which is mind, mentality, mentation, heart, lucidity, the mind-base, the mind-faculty, consciousness, the aggregate of consciousness, and the corresponding element of mind-consciousness—
this is called "mind. This mind is accompanied by,
co-arisen with, conjoined with, and associated with this loving-kindness.
Therefore it is said: “with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness.
“One direction” means the eastern direction, or the western direction, or the northern direction, or the southern direction, or above, or below, or across, or the intermediate directions.
“Having pervaded” means having pervaded and having resolved upon [that pervasion].
“Dwells” (*viharati*) means: he moves about, conducts himself, protects, maintains, sustains, wanders, and dwells.
Therefore it is said, “he dwells.

“Likewise a second”: just as [he dwells] in one direction, so in a second direction, so in a third direction, so in a fourth direction, so above, so below, so across, so in the intermediate directions.
“Everywhere, in every way, throughout the entire world”— this means entirely, in all respects, in every manner, without remainder,
and without exception. This expression,
“everywhere, in every way, throughout the entire world,” is a term used to signify total inclusion.
Regarding the phrase “with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness”: therein, what is loving-kindness (*mettā*)?
That which is friendliness toward beings, the state of being friendly, the state of having been friendly, and the liberation of the mind through loving-kindness—this is called “loving-kindness.”
In this context, what is consciousness?
That which is consciousness, mind, mentation …pe… the element of mind-consciousness born thereof—
this is called "consciousness."
This mind is accompanied by, co-nascent with, conjoined with, and associated with this loving-kindness.
Therefore it is said: "with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness.

Regarding the term "vast": that which is vast is sublime; that which is sublime is immeasurable; that which is immeasurable is free from enmity; that which is free from enmity is free from affliction.
“Having pervaded” means having pervaded and resolved upon [the object].
“Dwells” means …pe… therefore it is said, “dwells.”
1.2. Compassion.
And how does a bhikkhu dwell pervading one direction with a mind imbued with compassion?
Just as, for example, having seen a person who is destitute and poorly provided for, one would feel compassion; so too...
In the same way, one pervades all beings with compassion.
In this context, what is compassion?
It is that which is compassion toward beings, the state of being compassionate, the state of having been compassionate, and the liberation of mind through compassion.
This is called “compassion” (karuṇā).
In this context, what is the mind (citta)?
That which is mind, mentation, ideation …pe… the corresponding element of mind-consciousness (tajjā-manoviññāṇadhātu).
This is called "mind.
This mind is accompanied by, co-arisen with, conjoined with, and associated with this compassion.
Therefore, it is said: "with a mind accompanied by compassion."
“One direction”: either the eastern direction, the western direction, the northern direction, the southern direction, or above, below, across, or the intermediate directions.
“Having pervaded”: having pervaded and resolved upon.
“Dwells”: he moves, conducts himself, protects, maintains, sustains, wanders, and dwells.
Therefore it is said, “he dwells.

“Likewise a second”: just as toward one direction, so toward a second direction, so toward a third direction, so toward a fourth direction, so above, so below, so across, so toward the intermediate directions.
“In every way, everywhere, the entire world”: in all ways, entirely, in every manner, without remainder, leaving nothing out.
The expression “in every way, for the sake of the welfare of all, the entire world” is a comprehensive statement.
Regarding the phrase “with a mind accompanied by compassion,” what therein is compassion?
That which is compassion toward beings, the state of being compassionate, the state of having been compassionate, and the liberation of mind through compassion—
this is called "compassion.
In this context, what is "mind"?
That which is mind, mentality, mentation … [as above] … the corresponding mind-consciousness element—
this is called "mind.
This mind is accompanied by, co-nascent with, conjoined with, and associated with this compassion.
Therefore it is said: "with a mind accompanied by compassion. "Vast" (vipula):

that which is vast is exalted (mahaggata); that which is exalted is immeasurable (appamāṇa); that which is immeasurable is free from enmity (avera); that which is free from enmity is free from ill will (abyāpajja).
"Having pervaded" (pharitvā): having pervaded, having resolved with confidence.
“He dwells” (*viharati*) … [as before] … therefore it is said, “he dwells. 1.3.
Sympathetic Joy (*muditā*).
And how does a bhikkhu dwell having pervaded one direction with a mind imbued with sympathetic joy?
Just as one would be joyful upon seeing a person who is dear and pleasing,
even so he pervades all beings with sympathetic joy.
In this context, what is sympathetic joy (*muditā*)?
That which is sympathetic joy toward sentient beings, the state of sympathetic joy, the being sympathetic with joy, and the liberation of mind through sympathetic joy—
this is called "sympathetic joy."
In this context, what is consciousness?
That which is consciousness, mind, mentation …pe… the element of mind-consciousness born thereof—
this is called "consciousness."
This mind is accompanied by, co-arisen with, conjoined with, and associated with this sympathetic joy (*muditā*).
Therefore it is said: "with a mind accompanied by sympathetic joy.
"One direction" means the eastern direction, or the western direction, or the northern direction, or the southern direction, or above, or below, or across, or the intermediate directions.
“Having pervaded” means having pervaded and resolved upon [the object].
“He dwells” ... [as before] ...
therefore it is said, “he dwells.”

“Likewise the second”: just as [he pervades] one direction, so too the second direction, so too the third direction, so too the fourth direction, so too above, so too below, so too across, so too the intermediate directions.
“Everywhere, in every way, the entire world”: this means entirely, in its totality, in every manner, all without exception or remainder;
it is a term used for exhaustive inclusion.
“Toward every being in every way throughout the entire world.
Regarding the phrase “with a mind accompanied by gladness,” what therein is gladness (*muditā*)?
It is that which is gladness toward beings, the state of being glad, the state of having been gladdened, and the liberation of the mind through gladness.
This is called "altruistic joy" (muditā).
In this context, what is the mind (citta)?
It is that which is the mind, the intellect, the mentation … [as before] … the corresponding element of mind-consciousness (tajjā-manoviññāṇadhātu).
This is called "the mind.
This mind is accompanied by, co-arisen with, conjoined with, and associated with this sympathetic joy.
Therefore it is said: "with a mind accompanied by sympathetic joy."
“Vipula” means that what is vast is sublime; what is sublime is immeasurable; what is immeasurable is free from enmity; what is free from enmity is free from ill will.
“Having pervaded” means having pervaded and resolved upon [the object].
“Dwells” ... [and so on] ... [as before].
Therefore it is said, “he dwells.
1.4. Equanimity:
And how does a bhikkhu dwell, having pervaded one direction with a mind accompanied by equanimity?
Just as one would remain equanimous upon seeing a person who is neither pleasing nor unpleasing,
even so does he pervade all beings with equanimity.
In this context, what is equanimity?
That which is equanimity toward beings, the state of being equanimous, the quality of being equanimous, and the liberation of mind through equanimity—
this is called “equanimity.
In this context, what is “mind”?
That which is mind, intellect, mentation … [as above] … the corresponding mind-consciousness element—
this is called "mind.
This mind is accompanied by, co-nascent with, conjoined with, and associated with this equanimity.
Therefore it is said: “with a mind accompanied by equanimity.
“One direction” means the eastern direction, or the western direction, or the northern direction, or the southern direction, or above, or below, or across, or the intermediate directions.
“Having pervaded” means having pervaded and resolved [upon].
“Dwells” (*viharati*)...
[as before] ...therefore it is said, “he dwells.
“Likewise a second”: just as in one direction, so in a second direction, so in a third direction, so in a fourth direction, so above, so below, so across, so in the intermediate directions.
“Everywhere, in every way, throughout the entire world”— this means entirely, in every respect, in all manners, without remainder,
without exception. This expression,
“everywhere, in every way, throughout the entire world,” is a term used to denote complete exhaustion.
"With a mind accompanied by equanimity": therein, what is equanimity?
That which is equanimity toward sentient beings, the state of being equanimous, the state of having equanimity, the liberation of the mind through equanimity—this is called "equanimity."
In this context, what is consciousness?
That which is consciousness, mind, mentation …pe… the element of mind-consciousness born thereof—
this is called "consciousness."
This mind is accompanied by this equanimity; it is co-nascent, conjoined, and associated with it.
Therefore, it is said: "with a mind accompanied by equanimity.

Regarding the term "vast": that which is vast is sublime; that which is sublime is immeasurable; that which is immeasurable is free from enmity; and that which is free from enmity is free from ill will.
“Having pervaded” means having pervaded and resolved upon [the mind].
“He dwells” means... by this it is said, “he dwells.”
The Exposition of the Discourses (Suttantabhājanīya). 2.
The Exposition of the Abhidhamma (Abhidhammabhājanīya). 2.1.
The Wholesome (Kusala).
The four immeasurables:
loving-kindness, compassion, appreciative joy, and equanimity.
Among these, what is loving-kindness?
Here, bhikkhus, at whatever time a bhikkhu, for the sake of rebirth in the form realm, develops the path, secluded from sensual pleasures... [as before] ...and,

having attained the first jhāna accompanied by loving-kindness, dwells therein— at that time, whatever is loving-kindness, the state of loving-kindness, the act of loving-kindness, and the liberation of mind through loving-kindness— this is called "loving-kindness."
The remaining factors are associated with loving-kindness (*mettā*).
In this context, what is loving-kindness?
Here, at the time when a monk develops the path for rebirth in the realm of form, following the subsiding of applied and sustained thought...
...pe... he enters and dwells in the second jhāna accompanied by loving-kindness;
whatever at that time is loving-kindness, the state of loving-kindness, the act of loving-kindness, the liberation of mind through loving-kindness—this is called "loving-kindness."
The remaining factors are associated with loving-kindness (*mettā*).
In this context, what is loving-kindness?

Here, at whatever time a monk develops the path for rebirth in the form realm, through the fading away of rapture (*pīti*) … [as detailed in the full formula] … [he dwells with a mind imbued with loving-kindness]. This is loving-kindness.

He enters and dwells in the third jhāna accompanied by loving-kindness. At that time, whatever is loving-kindness, the state of loving-kindness, the act of loving-kindness, and the liberation of mind through loving-kindness—this is called “loving-kindness.
All remaining phenomena are associated with loving-kindness.

Here, monks, at whatever time a monk, secluded from sensual pleasures... [as above] ...enters and dwells in the first jhāna accompanied by loving-kindness while developing the path for rebirth in the realm of form—
at that time, whatever is loving-kindness, the state of being loving, the act of being loving, and the liberation of mind through loving-kindness—
this is called "loving-kindness."
The remaining phenomena are associated with loving-kindness (*mettā*). Here,
at whatever time a bhikkhu develops the path for rebirth in the form realm, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states,
he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which is without applied thought, with sustained thought only, born of seclusion, and filled with rapture and happiness.

He dwells accompanied by loving-kindness; whatever at that time is loving-kindness, the act of loving-kindness, the state of loving-kindness, the liberation of mind through loving-kindness—this is called "loving-kindness.
All remaining phenomena are associated with loving-kindness.
Here, bhikkhu, at whatever time a bhikkhu develops the path for rebirth in the form realm, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought...

[he] enters and dwells in the third jhāna accompanied by loving-kindness. Whatever at that time is loving-kindness, the state of being loving-kind, the act of being loving-kind, the liberation of mind through loving-kindness—that is [the first constituent].
This is called “loving-kindness.
The remaining phenomena are associated with loving-kindness.
Here, at whatever time a bhikkhu develops the path for rebirth in the form realm, through the fading away of rapture … [as before] … he enters and dwells in the fourth [jhāna].

He enters and dwells in a jhāna accompanied by loving-kindness; whatever at that time is loving-kindness, the state of being loving-kindness, the act of being loving-kindness, and the liberation of mind through loving-kindness—this is called "loving-kindness.
All remaining phenomena are associated with loving-kindness.
In this context, what is compassion (*karuṇā*)?
Here, at whatever time a bhikkhu, for the sake of rebirth in the form realm, develops the path, secluded from sensual pleasures...

[as above] ...and enters and dwells in the first *jhāna* accompanied by compassion; whatever at that time is compassion, the state of being compassionate, the act of being compassionate, and the liberation of mind through compassion—that is compassion.
This is called "compassion.
The remaining phenomena are associated with compassion.
In this context, what is compassion?
Here, monks, at whatever time a monk develops the path for rebirth in the form realm, having transcended rapture ... [as before] ...

he enters and dwells in the second jhāna accompanied by compassion; whatever at that time is compassion, the state of being compassionate, the act of being compassionate, the liberation of mind through compassion—this is called "compassion."

The remaining factors are associated with compassion (*karuṇā*). In this context, what is compassion? Here, at whatever time a monk develops the path for rebirth in the form realm, through the fading away of rapture (*pīti*) … [as before] … [he dwells in the third jhāna]. This is called compassion. The remaining factors are associated with compassion. What are the remaining factors? They are: contact, feeling, perception, volition, mind, initial application, sustained application, decision, energy, mindfulness, equanimity, attention, faith, diligence, mindfulness, wisdom, concentration, root, path, faculty, power, enlightenment factor, and so forth. These are the remaining factors associated with compassion. Furthermore, there are other mental states that are associated with compassion; these are the remaining factors associated with compassion. One enters and dwells in the third jhāna accompanied by compassion; whatever at that time is compassion, the state of being compassionate, the quality of being compassionate, the liberation of mind through compassion—this is called "compassion.
All remaining phenomena are associated with compassion.
Here, bhikkhu, at whatever time a bhikkhu, secluded from sensual pleasures... attains and dwells in the first jhāna accompanied by compassion while developing the path for rebirth in the form realm—
at that time, whatever is compassion, the state of being compassionate, the act of being compassionate, and the liberation of mind through compassion— this is called "compassion."
The remaining states are associated with compassion. Here,
at whatever time a bhikkhu develops the path for rebirth in the form realm, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states,
he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which is without applied thought, with sustained thought only, born of seclusion, and filled with rapture and happiness.
He dwells accompanied by compassion; whatever at that time is compassion, the state of compassion, the act of compassion, the liberation of mind through compassion—this is called "compassion.
All remaining phenomena are associated with compassion.
Here, monks, at whatever time a monk develops the path for rebirth in the form realm, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought...

[he] enters and dwells in the third jhāna accompanied by compassion. Whatever at that time is compassion, the state of compassion, the act of being compassionate, the liberation of mind through compassion—this is it.
This is called "compassion" (*karuṇā*).
The remaining phenomena are associated with compassion.
Here, at whatever time a bhikkhu develops the path for rebirth in the form realm, through the fading away of rapture … [as before] … the fourth [jhāna].

One enters and dwells in a jhāna accompanied by compassion; whatever at that time is compassion, the state of compassion, the act of being compassionate, and the liberation of mind through compassion—this is called "compassion.
All remaining phenomena are associated with compassion.
In this regard, what is sympathetic joy (*muditā*)?
Here, at whatever time a bhikkhu develops the path for rebirth in the realm of form, secluded from sensual pleasures...

[as before] ...he enters and dwells in the first *jhāna* accompanied by sympathetic joy; that which at that time is sympathetic joy, the state of sympathetic joy, the nature of sympathetic joy, the liberation of mind through sympathetic joy.
This is called "altruistic joy" (muditā).
All remaining phenomena are associated with altruistic joy.
In this context, what is altruistic joy?
Here, bhikkhu, at whatever time a bhikkhu develops the path for rebirth in the form realm, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought,
he enters and dwells in the second jhāna accompanied by sympathetic joy; whatever at that time is sympathetic joy,
the state of sympathetic joy, the being of sympathetic joy, and the liberation of mind through sympathetic joy— this is [sympathetic joy].
This is called "altruistic joy" (muditā).
All remaining phenomena are associated with altruistic joy.
In this context, what is altruistic joy?
Here, bhikkhus, at whatever time a bhikkhu develops the path for rebirth in the form realm, and through the fading away of rapture ... [as above] ...

enters and dwells in the third jhāna accompanied by gladness; whatever at that time is gladness, the state of being gladdened, the quality of being gladdened, the gladness-liberation of mind—this is called "gladness."
The remaining phenomena are associated with sympathetic joy (*muditā*).
Here, at whatever time a bhikkhu, for the sake of rebirth in the realm of form, develops the path, secluded from sensual pleasures...

[and so on] ...he enters and dwells in the first jhāna accompanied by sympathetic joy; at that time, whatever is sympathetic joy, the state of sympathetic joy, the nature of sympathetic joy, and the liberation of mind through sympathetic joy— *Avasesā dhammā muditāya sampayuttā.* *Idha bhikkhu yasmiṁ samaye rūpūpapattāya maggaṁ bhāveti vivicceva kāmehi …pe… paṭhamaṁ jhānaṁ upasampajja viharati muditāsahagataṁ, yā tasmiṁ samaye muditā muditāyanā muditāyitattaṁ muditācetovimutti—*
This is called "altruistic joy" (muditā).
All remaining mental factors are associated with altruistic joy.
Here, at whatever time a bhikkhu develops the path for rebirth in the realm of form, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from...
With the subsiding of applied thought, one dwells having attained the second jhāna, which is without applied thought, consists of sustained thought only, is born of seclusion,

and possesses rapture and happiness, accompanied by sympathetic joy (*muditā*). At that time, whatever is sympathetic joy, the state of sympathetic joy, the being sympathetic-joyful, and the liberation of mind through sympathetic joy— this is called "sympathetic joy."
The remaining phenomena are associated with sympathetic joy (*muditā*).
Here, at whatever time a bhikkhu develops the path for rebirth in the form realm, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought...
[as before] ...he enters and dwells in the third jhāna accompanied by sympathetic joy; that which at that time is sympathetic joy—[is associated with sympathetic joy].
The basis for gladness, the state of being glad, and the liberation of the mind through gladness—
this is called "gladness.
All remaining phenomena are associated with gladness.
Here, monks, at whatever time a monk develops the path for rebirth in the form realm, and through the fading away of rapture...

[as above] ...he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna accompanied by sympathetic joy; whatever at that time is sympathetic joy, the state of sympathetic joy, the being sympathetic joyful, the liberation of mind through sympathetic joy—this is called "sympathetic joy."
The remaining phenomena are associated with sympathetic joy (*muditā*).
In that context, what is equanimity (*upekkhā*)?
Here, at whatever time a monk develops the path for rebirth in the form realm, through the abandoning of pleasure … [as before] … he attains the fourth [jhāna].
He enters and dwells in a jhāna accompanied by equanimity; whatever at that time is equanimity,
the state of being equanimous, the state of having equanimity, and the liberation of mind through equanimity—
this is called "equanimity."
The remaining states are associated with equanimity.
2.2. Resultant:
The four immeasurables—
Loving-kindness, compassion, gladness, and equanimity.
Therein, what is loving-kindness?

Here, at whatever time a bhikkhu, for the sake of rebirth in the form realm, develops the path, secluded from sensual pleasures … [as before] … he enters and dwells in the first jhāna accompanied by loving-kindness; at that time there is contact … [as before] … there is non-distraction.
These states are wholesome.

As a result of having performed and accumulated that very same wholesome karma of the fine-material sphere, he, quite secluded from sensual pleasures … attains and dwells in the first jhāna accompanied by loving-kindness; whatever at that time is loving-kindness—these states are wholesome.
Loving-kindness, the state of loving-kindness, the liberation of mind through loving-kindness—
this is called "loving-kindness.
All remaining phenomena are associated with loving-kindness.
In this regard, what is loving-kindness (*mettā*)?

Here, at whatever time a bhikkhu develops the path for rebirth in the form realm, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna accompanied by loving-kindness; at that time, there is contact (*phassa*).
... [as before] ... non-distraction arises.
These states are wholesome.

Through the performance and accumulation of that very same wholesome kamma of the fine-material sphere, as a result, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, ... [as before] ... the second jhāna arises. ... [as before] ...
the third jhāna …pe… the first jhāna …pe… the second jhāna …pe…

He enters and dwells in the third jhāna … and the fourth jhāna accompanied by loving-kindness. Whatever at that time is loving-kindness, the state of loving-kindness, the act of loving-kindness, and the liberation of mind through loving-kindness—
this is called “loving-kindness.”
The remaining factors are associated with loving-kindness (*mettā*).
In that regard, what is compassion (*karuṇā*)?

Here, at whatever time a bhikkhu, for the sake of rebirth in the form realm, develops the path—secluded from sensual pleasures... [as before] ...and, accompanied by compassion, enters and dwells in the first *jhāna*, at that time there is contact... [as before] ...there is non-distraction (*avikkhepa*).
These states are wholesome.
As a result of having performed and accumulated that very wholesome karma pertaining to the fine-material sphere, he—secluded from sensual pleasures...
enters and dwells in the first jhāna accompanied by compassion; whatever at that time is compassion, these are wholesome states.
Compassion, the state of being compassionate, and the liberation of mind through compassion—
this is called "compassion.
All remaining phenomena are associated with compassion.
In this regard, what is compassion (*karuṇā*)?

Here, at whatever time a bhikkhu develops the path for rebirth in the form realm, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna accompanied by compassion; at that time, there is contact.
... [as before] ... there is non-distraction.
These states are wholesome.

Through having performed and accumulated that very wholesome karma of the fine-material sphere, as a result of the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, ... [as before] ... he enters upon the second jhāna, ... [as before] ...
the third jhāna …pe… the first jhāna …pe… the second jhāna …pe…

He enters and dwells in the third jhāna … and the fourth jhāna accompanied by compassion. Whatever at that time is compassion, the state of being compassionate, the act of being compassionate, the liberation of mind through compassion—
this is called "compassion."
The remaining factors are associated with compassion.
In this context, what is sympathetic joy (*muditā*)?

Here, at whatever time a bhikkhu, for the sake of rebirth in the form realm, develops the path, secluded from sensual pleasures... [as before] ...and, having attained the first *jhāna* accompanied by sympathetic joy, dwells therein—at that time there is contact... [as before] ...there is non-distraction.
These states are wholesome.

As the result of having performed and accumulated that very wholesome karma pertaining to the fine-material sphere, he—quite secluded from sensual pleasures … enters and dwells in the first jhāna accompanied by sympathetic joy; whatever at that time is sympathetic joy.
The basis for gladness, the state of being glad, and the liberation of the mind through gladness—
this is called “gladness.
All remaining phenomena are associated with gladness.
In this regard, what is sympathetic joy (*muditā*)?

Here, at whatever time a bhikkhu develops the path for rebirth in the realm of form, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna accompanied by sympathetic joy; at that time, there is contact.
...pe... there is non-distraction.
These states are wholesome.

Through the performance and accumulation of that very same wholesome karma of the fine-material sphere, as a result [of its ripening], with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, ...pe... the second jhāna ...pe...
the third jhāna …pe… the first jhāna …pe… the second jhāna …pe…

He enters and dwells in the third jhāna … and the fourth jhāna accompanied by sympathetic joy. Whatever at that time is sympathetic joy, the state of being sympathetic, the state of having been sympathetic, and the liberation of mind through sympathetic joy—
this is called “sympathetic joy.”
The remaining phenomena are associated with sympathetic joy (*muditā*).
In this context, what is equanimity (*upekkhā*)?
Here, at whatever time a bhikkhu develops the path for rebirth in the form realm, through the abandoning of pleasure … [as before] … he attains the fourth [jhāna].
He dwells having attained the jhāna accompanied by equanimity; at that time there is contact …pe… there is non-distraction.
These states are wholesome.
Through the performance and accumulation of that very same wholesome karma of the fine-material sphere, its result arises through the abandoning of pleasure …pe… [and so on].
With the abandoning of suffering … [and so on] … he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, accompanied by equanimity.
Whatever at that time is equanimity, the state of being equanimous, the state of having equanimity, the liberation of mind through equanimity—
this is called “equanimity.”
The remaining states are associated with equanimity.
2.3. Functional:
The four illimitables—
Loving-kindness, compassion, appreciative joy, and equanimity.
Therein, what is loving-kindness?
Here, at whatever time a bhikkhu develops a fine-material-sphere jhāna that is functional, neither wholesome nor unwholesome.
And it is not the ripening of kamma, but rather that which, secluded from sensual pleasures...

having attained and dwelling in the first jhāna accompanied by loving-kindness (*mettā*); whatever at that time is loving-kindness, the state of being loving, the quality of loving-kindness, and the liberation of mind through loving-kindness—this is called "loving-kindness."
The remaining states are associated with loving-kindness (*mettā*).
In this context, what is loving-kindness?

Here, at whatever time a bhikkhu develops a form-sphere jhāna that is functional (*kiriya*), neither wholesome nor unwholesome, and not the result of kamma—a pleasant abiding in this very life—wherein, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna... [and so forth].
the third jhāna …pe… the first jhāna …pe… the second jhāna …pe…

He enters and dwells in the third jhāna … and the fourth jhāna accompanied by loving-kindness. At that time, whatever is loving-kindness, the state of being loving-kindness, the state of having practiced loving-kindness, and the liberation of mind through loving-kindness—
this is called "loving-kindness."
The remaining phenomena are associated with loving-kindness (*mettā*).
Therein, what is compassion (*karuṇā*)? ... [as before] ...
Therein, what is sympathetic joy (*muditā*)? ... [as before] ...
In this context, what is equanimity? Here,
at whatever time a bhikkhu develops a form-sphere jhāna that is functional— neither wholesome nor unwholesome,
and not the result of kamma— a pleasant dwelling in the present life, through the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain...
...pe... he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna accompanied by equanimity;
whatever at that time is equanimity, the state of being equanimous, the quality of being equanimous, the liberation of mind through equanimity—this is called "equanimity."
The remaining states are associated with equanimity.
This concludes the Exposition according to the Abhidhamma. 3.
The Interrogation by Questions.
The four immeasurables:
Here, a bhikkhu dwells pervading one quarter with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth;

thus above, below, across, everywhere, and to all as to himself, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, vast, exalted, measureless, and free from enmity and ill will.
He dwells pervading the world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness—vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will.
With a mind imbued with compassion, he dwells pervading one direction, likewise the second, likewise the third, and likewise the fourth;
thus above, below, across, everywhere, and to all as himself, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with compassion.
He dwells having pervaded with a mind that is vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will.
With a mind imbued with gladness, he dwells pervading one quarter, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth;
thus above, below, across, everywhere, and to all as to himself, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with gladness.
He dwells having pervaded with a mind that is vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will.
With a mind imbued with equanimity, he dwells pervading one direction, likewise the second, likewise the third, and likewise the fourth;
thus above, below, across, everywhere, and in all respects, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with equanimity.
He dwells having pervaded [the world] with a mind that is vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will. Regarding the four immeasurables (*appamaññā*):

how many are wholesome (*kusala*), how many are unwholesome (*akusala*), and how many are indeterminate (*abyākata*)? …pe… How many are with conflict (*saraṇa*), and how many are without conflict (*araṇa*)?
3.1. The Triads.
They may be wholesome, or they may be indeterminate.
Three of the immeasurables are associated with pleasant feeling; equanimity is associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
They may be results, or they may be of a nature to produce results, or they may be neither results nor of a nature to produce results.
They may be acquired and subject to clinging, or they may be unacquired but subject to clinging.
They are not defiled and are not objects of defilement.

Three of the immeasurables may be accompanied by both initial and sustained application, or they may be without initial application and with sustained application only, or they may be without both initial and sustained application.
Equanimity is without applied thought and without sustained thought.

Three of the immeasurables may be accompanied by rapture, may be accompanied by pleasure, but are not accompanied by equanimity; they may also be such that it cannot be said that they are accompanied by rapture.
Equanimity is accompanied by equanimity.
They are not to be abandoned either by vision or by cultivation.
They do not have roots that are to be abandoned either by vision or by cultivation.
They may be conducive to accumulation, or they may be neither conducive to accumulation nor conducive to diminution.
Neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee states. Lofty. They should not be said to have limited objects, nor lofty objects, nor immeasurable objects.
The intermediate [states] are indeterminate.
They should not be described as having the Path as their object, nor as having the Path as their cause, nor as having the Path as their predominance.
They may have arisen, they may not have arisen, or they may be in the process of arising.
They may be past, they may be future, or they may be present.
They should not be described as having a past object, nor as having a future object, nor as having a present object.
They may be internal, they may be external, or they may be both internal and external.
They have external objects.
They are non-manifest and non-reacting.
Hetugocchaka (The Group on Roots) Loving-kindness is a root; the other three immeasurables are not roots; they are accompanied by roots and associated with roots.
Loving-kindness is both a root and accompanied by roots;
the other three immeasurables should not be said to be "both roots and accompanied by roots," but rather they are "accompanied by roots but are not roots.
Loving-kindness is both a root and associated with roots.
The three immeasurables (appamaññā) should not be described as "both roots and associated with roots," but rather as "associated with roots and not roots.
The three immeasurables are not roots, yet they are accompanied by roots (sahetuka).
Loving-kindness (mettā) should not be described as "neither root nor accompanied by roots," nor as "neither root nor without roots" (ahetuka).
3.2.2. The Minor Intermediate Dyads:
With conditions; conditioned; non-demonstrable; non-reactive; immaterial; mundane; cognizable by something; not cognizable by something. 3.2.3.
The Group on Taints (Āsava-gocchaka)
The taints (āsava) are not associated with taints; they are dissociated from taints. They should not be described as "both taints and associated with taints";

rather, they are associated with taints but are not themselves taints. They should not be described as "both taints and associated with taints," nor as "associated with taints but not themselves taints.
Those things dissociated from taints are associated with taints.
13.3.2.4. The Group on Fetters (Saṃyojana-gocchaka), etc.
There are no fetters … [and so on] … there are no ties … [and so on] …
There are no floods ...
[and so on] ... there are no yokes ... [and so on] ... there are no hindrances ... [and so on] ...
...no perversions ... 3.2.10.
The Greater Pair:
With an object, not consciousness, mental factors, associated with consciousness, conjoined with consciousness, generated by consciousness.

They are co-existent with consciousness, they follow after consciousness, they are conjoined with and produced by consciousness, they are co-existent with what is conjoined with and produced by consciousness, they follow after what is conjoined with and produced by consciousness;
they are external, not derived, and may be either clung-to or not clung-to.
13.3.2.11. The Group on Clinging (Upādāna-gocchaka), etc.
There are no clinging-aggregates …pe… no defilements …pe… they are not to be abandoned by vision,
nor to be abandoned by cultivation; they do not have roots to be abandoned by vision, nor do they have roots to be abandoned by cultivation.
Three immeasurables may be with applied thought, or they may be without applied thought;
equanimity is without applied thought.
Three immeasurables may be with sustained thought, or they may be without sustained thought.
Equanimity is without applied thought.
Three of the immeasurables may be accompanied by joy, or they may be without joy;
equanimity is without joy.
Three immeasurables may be accompanied by rapture, or they may not be accompanied by rapture;
equanimity is not accompanied by rapture.
Three immeasurables are accompanied by pleasure; equanimity is not accompanied by pleasure.

Equanimity is accompanied by equanimity; the other three immeasurables are not accompanied by equanimity. They do not belong to the sense sphere; they belong to the fine-material sphere; they do not belong to the immaterial sphere. They are included within the mundane, they do not lead to liberation, they are indefinite, they have something higher than themselves, and they are without conflict.
This concludes the interrogation. The Analysis of the Immeasurables is finished.
